fields.Question:
Postgres, default READ COMMITTED. Two requests run this at the same moment for the last seat (seats_left = 1). The app computes the new value itself.

BEGIN;
SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 7;
-- app: if seats_left > 0
UPDATE events SET seats_left = 0 WHERE id = 7;
INSERT INTO tickets ...;
COMMIT;

What happens?
fields.Choices:
The transaction makes the read and the write atomic, so the second request fails
Both requests sell the seat, because both reads see 1 before either commits
The second UPDATE blocks, then aborts with a serialization error
Postgres detects the read-check-write conflict and rolls back one transaction
fields.Correct: Both requests sell the seat, because both reads see 1 before either commits
fields.Explanation:
A transaction does not lock rows it only reads. At READ COMMITTED both SELECTs see 1, both pass the check, and the second UPDATE waits for the first, then writes 0 again: two tickets for one seat.

Atomicity means all or nothing on failure, not mutual exclusion. Serialization errors only happen at REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE. Postgres never checks app-side logic at READ COMMITTED.
fields.Hint: A plain SELECT takes no row lock.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Dealing with Contention (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/patterns/dealing-with-contention)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: Same last-seat race. You want the smallest correct fix with one database round trip and no new infrastructure. Which do you pick?
fields.Choices:
UPDATE events SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND seats_left > 0, then check the affected row count
Wrap the SELECT and UPDATE in a Redis distributed lock keyed by event id
Switch the whole database to SERIALIZABLE isolation
Cache seats_left in Redis and decrement the cache first
fields.Correct: UPDATE events SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND seats_left > 0, then check the affected row count
fields.Explanation:
The conditional UPDATE does the check and the write in one atomic statement on a locked row. The second writer re-evaluates the WHERE after the first commits, matches 0 rows, and you report sold out.

A Redis lock adds a dependency and its own failure modes (expiry, failover) for a problem the row lock already solves. SERIALIZABLE everywhere costs retries on every transaction. A cache decrement is not the source of truth and can drift from the database.
fields.Hint: Put the check inside the WHERE clause.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: Postgres READ COMMITTED. T1 runs SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE, reads 1, sets it to 0 and has not committed yet. T2 runs the same SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. What does T2 get?
fields.Choices:
T2 reads 1 immediately from its own snapshot
T2 fails at once with a lock not available error
T2 reads 1 and only blocks later at its UPDATE
T2 waits until T1 commits, then reads seats_left = 0
fields.Correct: T2 waits until T1 commits, then reads seats_left = 0
fields.Explanation:
FOR UPDATE takes a row lock, so T2 blocks on it. At READ COMMITTED, once T1 commits, Postgres re-checks the updated row version and returns it, so T2 sees 0.

Reading the old value without waiting is what a plain SELECT does. Failing at once is FOR UPDATE NOWAIT. Blocking only at the UPDATE describes a plain SELECT followed by UPDATE, which is the original race.
fields.Hint: The lock is taken at read time.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: SELECT (including FOR UPDATE and SKIP LOCKED) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question:
Optimistic locking on a documents table:

UPDATE documents
SET body = $1, version = version + 1
WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3;

The statement reports 0 rows updated. What should the API do?
fields.Choices:
Insert a new row, since 0 rows means the document does not exist
Do nothing, the database queues the update and applies it after the other writer
Treat it as a conflict: someone changed the row since you read it, so reload and retry or return 409
Retry the same UPDATE with the same version until it succeeds
fields.Correct: Treat it as a conflict: someone changed the row since you read it, so reload and retry or return 409
fields.Explanation:
The version you read is stale, so another writer won. Reload, merge or reapply the change, or surface a conflict to the user.

Inserting would create a duplicate of an existing document. Databases do not queue failed conditional updates. Retrying with the same old version will match 0 rows forever.
fields.Hint: The version column no longer matches.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Dealing with Contention (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/patterns/dealing-with-contention)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You are choosing between optimistic version checks and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. In which workload is pessimistic locking clearly the better choice?
fields.Choices:
A wiki where two people rarely edit the same page at once
A flash sale where thousands of buyers hit the same inventory row within seconds
User profile edits that only the owner makes
A mobile app syncing notes that may be edited offline for hours
fields.Correct: A flash sale where thousands of buyers hit the same inventory row within seconds
fields.Explanation:
Under heavy contention on one row, optimistic writers mostly fail and retry, so retries pile up and throughput collapses. Queueing on a row lock is cheaper.

Rare conflicts (wiki, own profile) favour optimistic: no locks held, little retry cost. Offline edits cannot hold a database lock for hours at all, so they need version checks or merge logic.
fields.Hint: Count how often the conflict actually happens.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Dealing with Contention (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/patterns/dealing-with-contention)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Ten workers pull jobs from a Postgres jobs table. You need each job claimed by exactly one worker and workers must not wait on each other. Which claim query fits?
fields.Choices:
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' LIMIT 1, then UPDATE jobs SET status = 'taken' WHERE id = it
fields.Correct: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
fields.Explanation:
SKIP LOCKED makes each worker pass over rows another worker holds and lock the next free one, so claims are exclusive and nobody blocks.

Plain FOR UPDATE makes every worker queue on the same first row. NOWAIT raises an error instead of moving on. A plain SELECT then UPDATE lets two workers read the same row and both take it.
fields.Hint: Skip rows that are already claimed.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: SELECT (including FOR UPDATE and SKIP LOCKED) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html)

fields.Question: A worker takes a Redis lock with a 10 second TTL, then hits a 15 second GC pause. The lock expires, a second worker takes it, and both write to the database. What actually prevents the corrupted write?
fields.Choices:
A longer TTL, such as 60 seconds
Redlock across five independent Redis nodes
Having the worker check it still holds the lock just before writing
A fencing token: an increasing number from the lock that the database checks and rejects if older
fields.Correct: A fencing token: an increasing number from the lock that the database checks and rejects if older
fields.Explanation:
Only the resource can reject a stale holder. With a monotonically increasing token stored on the row, the paused worker's write carries an older token and the database refuses it.

Any TTL can be exceeded by a pause or network delay. Redlock still relies on timing and does not stop a paused client. Checking before writing leaves a gap: the pause can happen right after the check.
fields.Hint: The storage must be able to say no.
fields.Source:
How to do distributed locking, Martin Kleppmann, 2016 (https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)
Redis Documentation: Distributed locks with Redis (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/patterns/distributed-locks/)

fields.Question: A like counter is one row updated with likes = likes + 1. A viral post drives 5,000 increments per second and requests queue on the row lock. Exact counts can lag by a few seconds. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before each increment
Switch to optimistic locking with a version column
Spread increments over N counter rows (or buffer them) and sum on read
Raise the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE
fields.Correct: Spread increments over N counter rows (or buffer them) and sum on read
fields.Explanation:
The bottleneck is one row lock per increment. Sharded counter rows or batched increments from a queue cut contention by N, and reads sum a few rows or a cached total.

FOR UPDATE takes the same lock the atomic UPDATE already takes. Optimistic locking turns waiting into failed retries, which is worse at this contention. Higher isolation adds aborts and does not remove the single hot row.
fields.Hint: One row cannot take unlimited writes.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Dealing with Contention (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/patterns/dealing-with-contention)
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-sharding.html)

fields.Question: Postgres. Bookings have room_id and a stay as a daterange. Two concurrent requests must never book overlapping stays for the same room. Which guarantee holds under concurrency without app-level locking?
fields.Choices:
A UNIQUE constraint on (room_id, start_date)
An exclusion constraint: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, stay WITH &&)
Check for overlapping rows in the app, then INSERT in the same transaction
A B-tree index on (room_id, start_date, end_date)
fields.Correct: An exclusion constraint: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, stay WITH &&)
fields.Explanation:
An exclusion constraint rejects any new row whose room matches and whose range overlaps an existing one, enforced by the database even for concurrent inserts. The = on room_id needs the btree_gist extension.

UNIQUE on the start date only blocks identical starts, not overlaps. Check-then-insert at READ COMMITTED races because neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted row. An index speeds lookups but enforces nothing.
fields.Hint: Let the constraint compare ranges.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

fields.Question:
Postgres READ COMMITTED. Balance is 500. Two transactions run concurrently and both commit:

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 1;

What is the final balance?
fields.Choices:
300
400
500
One transaction fails, so 400
fields.Explanation:
The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock, then re-reads the committed 400 and writes 300. Doing the arithmetic in SQL avoids the lost update.

400 is the lost update you get when the app reads 500 and writes back a computed value. 500 would mean both were lost. At READ COMMITTED a simple conflicting UPDATE waits, it does not fail.
fields.Hint: The second writer re-reads the row after the lock is released.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: Walk through how you prevent double booking of seats in a ticketing system, from seat hold to payment.
fields.Answer:
Hold a seat with a conditional write: UPDATE seats SET status = 'held', held_by = $u, hold_expires = now() + interval '10 minutes' WHERE id = $s AND (status = 'free' OR hold_expires < now()), and check the row count. Payment confirms with another conditional UPDATE from held by this user to sold. Expired holds free themselves through the expiry check or a sweeper.

Mention the alternatives and why: FOR UPDATE for short critical sections, optimistic version checks when contention is low, a Redis hold with TTL only as a fast path while the database stays the source of truth. Make payment idempotent so a retried confirm cannot sell twice.
fields.Hint: Conditional writes plus an expiring hold.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)
Hello Interview: Dealing with Contention (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/patterns/dealing-with-contention)

fields.Question:
A payment endpoint dedups retries like this:

SELECT 1 FROM payments WHERE idem_key = $1;
-- if no row: charge card, then
INSERT INTO payments (idem_key, ...) ...;

A client times out and retries, so two requests with the same key arrive together. What prevents a double charge?
fields.Choices:
Running the SELECT and INSERT in one transaction at READ COMMITTED
Keeping an in-memory set of seen keys on each API server
Adding a regular index on idem_key so the SELECT is fast
A UNIQUE constraint on the key, and inserting the key row before calling the card network
fields.Correct: A UNIQUE constraint on the key, and inserting the key row before calling the card network
fields.Explanation:
Inserting the key first makes the database pick one winner: the second insert hits the unique violation and does not charge. The row then records the in-flight state and later the stored response.

A transaction does not stop both SELECTs from seeing no row. In-memory sets miss retries routed to another server or after a restart. A plain index makes the race faster, not impossible.
fields.Hint: Let the database pick the winner.
fields.Source:
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, Brandur Leach (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
PostgreSQL Documentation: INSERT (ON CONFLICT) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)

fields.Question: Your idempotency layer has a row for key K in state in_progress because the first request is still talking to the bank. A retry with K arrives. Following Stripe's approach, what do you return?
fields.Choices:
Process the retry as a new payment
Return 200 with an empty body
An error such as 409 Conflict telling the client the original request is still in progress
Delete the in_progress row and start over
fields.Correct: An error such as 409 Conflict telling the client the original request is still in progress
fields.Explanation:
Stripe returns a conflict for concurrent use of the same key. The client retries later and then gets the stored result.

Processing again is the double charge you are preventing. A 200 with no result lies about the outcome. Deleting the in-flight row lets the duplicate run alongside the original.
fields.Hint: The first attempt has not finished yet.
fields.Source:
Stripe API Reference: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, Brandur Leach (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

fields.Question: Your service charges a card through a provider that supports idempotency keys, then crashes before saving the result. The client retries. How do you avoid charging twice?
fields.Choices:
Wrap the provider call in the database transaction so a crash rolls it back
Send the provider the same idempotency key on the retry so it returns the original charge
Mark the attempt failed on restart and charge again
Use two-phase commit between your database and the provider
fields.Correct: Send the provider the same idempotency key on the retry so it returns the original charge
fields.Explanation:
The external call cannot be undone by your rollback, so dedup has to reach the provider. Deriving the provider key from your own key makes the retry safe, and your row moves from in_progress to done once the result is saved.

A local rollback does not reverse a charge that already happened. Charging again is the bug. Payment providers do not take part in 2PC with your database.
fields.Hint: Your rollback cannot reach the bank.
fields.Source:
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, Brandur Leach (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
Every question I was asked in Stripe's system design interview (https://medium.com/@emilyhustlenyc/every-question-i-was-asked-in-stripes-system-design-interview-f6f19c2e62d6)

fields.Question: A client reuses idempotency key K, but the second request has amount 50 where the first had 30. Following Stripe's behaviour, what should the server do?
fields.Choices:
Reject it with an error, because the parameters differ from the original request
Process it as a new payment because the body changed
Return the stored response for the 30 payment as if it were a match
Update the original payment to 50
fields.Correct: Reject it with an error, because the parameters differ from the original request
fields.Explanation:
Stripe compares parameters with the original and errors if they differ, which catches client bugs that reuse keys.

Treating it as new breaks the key's meaning. Silently replaying the old response hides the bug and the client thinks 50 was charged. Mutating the original changes a completed payment.
fields.Hint: A key names one specific request.
fields.Source: Stripe API Reference: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

fields.Question: After saving an order you must publish OrderCreated to Kafka. A crash between the two steps must never lose the event or publish one for an order that was not saved. What do you do?
fields.Choices:
Publish to Kafka first, then commit the order
Commit the order, then publish with retries in the request handler
Use a two-phase commit across Postgres and Kafka
Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it to Kafka afterwards
fields.Correct: Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it to Kafka afterwards
fields.Explanation:
One local transaction writes both the order and the outbox row, so they exist together or not at all. A relay or CDC process publishes and may resend, so consumers must be idempotent.

Publishing first can announce an order that then fails to commit. Publishing after commit loses the event if the process dies in between. Kafka does not join an XA transaction with Postgres.
fields.Hint: Make it one local write.
fields.Source:
Pattern: Transactional outbox, Chris Richardson, microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)
Debezium Documentation: PostgreSQL connector (https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/connectors/postgresql.html)

fields.Question: A multi-tenant API lets each merchant send its own idempotency keys, which are free-form strings. Which constraint is right?
fields.Choices:
UNIQUE (idem_key)
UNIQUE (idem_key, created_at)
UNIQUE (merchant_id, idem_key)
A non-unique index on idem_key
fields.Correct: UNIQUE (merchant_id, idem_key)
fields.Explanation:
Keys are only meaningful per client. Scoping by merchant stops one merchant's key from blocking or replaying another merchant's request, while still deduping within a merchant.

A global unique key lets two merchants who both send order-1 collide, and could leak a response across tenants. Adding created_at makes every retry unique, so nothing is deduped. A non-unique index enforces nothing.
fields.Hint: Whose key is it?
fields.Source: Stripe API Reference: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

fields.Question: Design the idempotency layer for a POST /payments endpoint that calls an external card processor.
fields.Answer:
Table keyed by UNIQUE (account_id, idem_key) storing request hash, state (started, external_called, done), response code and body. On a request, insert the row first: a unique violation means look up the existing row, return the stored response if done, 409 if in progress, and an error if the request hash differs.

Call the processor with a key derived from yours so its side dedups. Save each step as you go so a retry resumes from the last saved step. Expire keys after about 24 hours. Publish events through an outbox in the same transaction.
fields.Hint: Insert first, store the response, dedup at the provider.
fields.Source:
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, Brandur Leach (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
Stripe API Reference: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

fields.Question: Postgres 16 has a B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at), with millions of distinct customers. A query filters only on created_at = $1. How does the index help?
fields.Choices:
It is used fully, since created_at is part of the index
It cannot seek on created_at, so at best the planner scans the whole index
Postgres reorders the index columns to match the query
It seeks on created_at and skips customer_id
fields.Correct: It cannot seek on created_at, so at best the planner scans the whole index
fields.Explanation:
Entries are sorted by customer_id first, so created_at values are scattered across the whole index. Without the leading column there is no range to seek to.

Being in the index is not enough, column order matters. Postgres never reorders index columns. Skip scan arrived only in Postgres 18, and even there it pays off only when the leading column has few distinct values.
fields.Hint: Think of a phone book sorted by last name.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

fields.Question:
Query:

SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = $2
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Which single index lets Postgres read just 20 entries with no sort step?
fields.Choices:
(tenant_id, status, created_at)
(created_at, tenant_id, status)
(tenant_id, created_at, status)
Separate indexes on tenant_id, status and created_at
fields.Correct: (tenant_id, status, created_at)
fields.Explanation:
Equality columns first, then the sort column. The index lands on the tenant and status block, which is already ordered by created_at, and reads the last 20 backwards.

Leading with created_at walks the whole time order filtering rows. With created_at second the order is right but status is checked entry by entry, reading extra rows for rare statuses. Separate indexes need a bitmap combine and then a sort.
fields.Hint: Equality, then sort.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

fields.Question: Query: WHERE status = 'failed' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'. Which composite index is better?
fields.Choices:
(created_at, status)
Either, column order does not matter for AND
(created_at) alone
(status, created_at)
fields.Correct: (status, created_at)
fields.Explanation:
With the equality column first, matching rows are one contiguous slice: status = failed, then created_at in range.

With the range first, the scan covers every status in the last day and filters status per entry. Order matters for B-trees, AND or not. created_at alone reads every status in the window.
fields.Hint: Range columns go last.
fields.Source:
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)

fields.Question: Hot query: SELECT email FROM users WHERE org_id = $1. There is an index on org_id, but EXPLAIN shows many heap fetches. Which change can let Postgres answer from the index alone?
fields.Choices:
Add a separate index on email
Replace the index with a hash index on org_id
CREATE INDEX ON users (org_id) INCLUDE (email)
Increase work_mem
fields.Correct: CREATE INDEX ON users (org_id) INCLUDE (email)
fields.Explanation:
INCLUDE stores email in the index leaf, so an index-only scan can return it. Postgres still checks the visibility map, so recently changed pages may need heap visits until VACUUM runs.

A separate email index does not help a lookup by org_id. Hash indexes do not support index-only scans. work_mem affects sorts and hashes, not heap fetches.
fields.Hint: Put the selected column in the index.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)

fields.Question: Login runs WHERE lower(email) = lower($1). There is a B-tree index on email, yet Postgres does a sequential scan. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Run ANALYZE on the table
An index on lower(email)
A hash index on email
Rewrite the query with ILIKE
fields.Correct: An index on lower(email)
fields.Explanation:
The index stores raw email values, so it cannot match an expression on the column. An expression index stores lower(email) and the planner can use it for that exact expression.

ANALYZE refreshes statistics but cannot make an index on email match lower(email). A hash index on email has the same mismatch. ILIKE cannot use a plain B-tree either.
fields.Hint: The index must match the expression.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Indexes on Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-expressional.html)

fields.Question: MySQL InnoDB, primary key is a random UUIDv4. Insert throughput drops as the table grows past memory. What is the main cause?
fields.Choices:
Random keys land all over the clustered index, causing page splits and reads of cold pages
UUIDs are 16 bytes, so comparisons are too slow
InnoDB has to hash each UUID before inserting it
The table needs an extra secondary index on the UUID
fields.Correct: Random keys land all over the clustered index, causing page splits and reads of cold pages
fields.Explanation:
InnoDB stores rows in primary key order. Random keys insert into random leaf pages, so once the working set exceeds the buffer pool most inserts read a page from disk and split pages. Time-ordered keys (UUIDv7, bigint) append to the right edge.

Comparing 16 bytes costs little next to disk reads. InnoDB does not hash the primary key. The primary key is already the clustered index, and another index adds write cost.
fields.Hint: Where does each new row go physically?
fields.Source:
MySQL Reference Manual: Clustered and Secondary Indexes (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-index-types.html)
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)

fields.Question: Postgres. You need fast lookups for WHERE created_at BETWEEN $1 AND $2 ORDER BY created_at. Which index type?
fields.Choices:
Hash
GIN
Either B-tree or hash, both support ranges
B-tree
fields.Correct: B-tree
fields.Explanation:
B-trees keep keys sorted, so they serve ranges and ORDER BY.

Hash indexes only support equality. GIN is for composite values such as arrays, jsonb and full-text search, not scalar ranges.
fields.Hint: You need order.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Index Types (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html)

fields.Question: A 200M row tasks table has about 0.5% rows with status = 'pending', and the worker queries only those. Which index gives the smallest, cheapest structure for that query?
fields.Choices:
CREATE INDEX ON tasks (status)
CREATE INDEX ON tasks (status, created_at)
CREATE INDEX ON tasks (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'
No index, status has too few distinct values to ever be useful
fields.Correct: CREATE INDEX ON tasks (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'
fields.Explanation:
A partial index holds only the 1M pending rows, so it is small, stays in cache, and done rows never touch it on update.

An index on status covers all 200M rows to serve 0.5%. The composite works but is equally huge. Low cardinality overall does not matter when the queried value is rare.
fields.Hint: Index only the rows you query.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Partial Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)

fields.Question: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a nested loop where the planner estimated rows=10 but actual rows=2000000, and the query takes minutes. What do you check first?
fields.Choices:
Add another index on the inner table
Planner statistics: run ANALYZE, or add extended statistics for correlated columns
Raise shared_buffers
Disable sequential scans globally
fields.Correct: Planner statistics: run ANALYZE, or add extended statistics for correlated columns
fields.Explanation:
A nested loop is a good plan for 10 rows and a terrible one for 2M. The estimate is off by 200,000x, so fix what the planner believes: stale stats or correlated predicates the planner treats as independent.

An index does not fix a wrong row count. More cache helps a little but the plan is still wrong. Disabling seq scans globally hides the cause and harms other queries.
fields.Hint: Compare estimated and actual rows.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Using EXPLAIN (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)

fields.Question: A feed pages with ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 20 and deep pages are slow, even with an index on (created_at, id). What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Keyset pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id) with the same ORDER BY and LIMIT 20
Add an index on id
Cache the COUNT(*) of the table
Increase LIMIT so fewer pages are needed
fields.Correct: Keyset pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id) with the same ORDER BY and LIMIT 20
fields.Explanation:
OFFSET still reads and throws away a million index entries. A keyset condition seeks straight to the last row seen and reads 20.

The existing index already covers the order, the cost is the skipped rows. Counting does not change the scan. Bigger pages only reduce how often you pay the same cost.
fields.Hint: Start from where the last page ended.
fields.Source: Use The Index, Luke: Paging Through Results (https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)

fields.Question: Keyset pagination uses WHERE created_at < $last ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Many rows share the same timestamp. What goes wrong?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, timestamps are unique enough
The query falls back to a full table scan
Rows are returned in random order but none are lost
Rows with the boundary timestamp get skipped, so add a unique tiebreaker such as id to the key
fields.Correct: Rows with the boundary timestamp get skipped, so add a unique tiebreaker such as id to the key
fields.Explanation:
If page 1 ends in the middle of rows sharing one timestamp, the strict < skips the rest of them. Compare (created_at, id) and order by both so every row has a unique position.

Bulk inserts and coarse clocks often produce equal timestamps. The plan does not change. Rows are lost, not only reordered.
fields.Hint: Your sort key must be unique.
fields.Source: Use The Index, Luke: Paging Through Results (https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)

fields.Question: Product asks to move a table view from OFFSET to keyset pagination. What do you give up?
fields.Choices:
Stable results when rows are inserted while paging
Using an index for the query
Jumping straight to an arbitrary page number such as page 500
Sorting in descending order
fields.Correct: Jumping straight to an arbitrary page number such as page 500
fields.Explanation:
Keyset needs the last row of the previous page, so it supports next and previous, not random page jumps.

Keyset is more stable under inserts than OFFSET, which shifts rows between pages. It is the variant that uses the index well. Descending order works with a matching index or a backward scan.
fields.Hint: You need a bookmark from the previous page.
fields.Source: Use The Index, Luke: Paging Through Results (https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)

fields.Question:
Postgres REPEATABLE READ. Rule: at least one doctor on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Each runs at the same time:

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call;
-- sees 2, so it is safe to leave
UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false
WHERE name = $me;
COMMIT;

What happens?
fields.Choices:
The second COMMIT fails with a serialization error
Both commit and nobody is on call
The second UPDATE blocks until the first commits, then sees count 1
REPEATABLE READ prevents this because both read the same rows
fields.Correct: Both commit and nobody is on call
fields.Explanation:
This is write skew. Each transaction reads a snapshot showing 2 doctors and updates a different row, so no write conflicts and both commit. Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and allows this.

A serialization error here needs SERIALIZABLE. The UPDATEs touch different rows, so neither blocks. Repeatable read keeps your reads stable, it does not check that other writers changed what you read.
fields.Hint: They update different rows.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Question: Same on-call write skew in Postgres. Which change actually prevents it?
fields.Choices:
Run SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failure, or lock the rows you counted with FOR UPDATE
Use READ COMMITTED instead
Add a UNIQUE constraint on doctors.name
Put both statements inside one transaction
fields.Correct: Run SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failure, or lock the rows you counted with FOR UPDATE
fields.Explanation:
SERIALIZABLE (SSI) detects the read-write dependency and aborts one transaction. Alternatively, select the on-call rows themselves with FOR UPDATE (count(*) cannot take FOR UPDATE): the second transaction blocks on the first, then re-checks at READ COMMITTED or gets a serialization error to retry at REPEATABLE READ.

READ COMMITTED is weaker. A unique name constraint has nothing to do with the count. They already run in transactions, and that alone does not help.
fields.Hint: Make the read conflict with the other write.
fields.Source:
Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: What are the default isolation levels of PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB?
fields.Choices:
Both SERIALIZABLE
PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, MySQL InnoDB READ COMMITTED
Both READ COMMITTED
PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ
fields.Correct: PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ
fields.Explanation:
Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED. InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, using consistent snapshots plus next-key locks for locking reads.

Neither defaults to SERIALIZABLE. The swapped pair is the common mix-up. Assuming both are READ COMMITTED misses that MySQL reads come from a transaction-wide snapshot.
fields.Hint: They differ.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
MySQL Reference Manual: Transaction Isolation Levels (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html)

fields.Question: Postgres REPEATABLE READ. T1 and T2 both read a row, then both UPDATE that same row. T1 commits first. What happens to T2?
fields.Choices:
T2 overwrites T1's change silently
T2 waits, then applies its update on top of T1's
T2 fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update
Both are rolled back as a deadlock
fields.Correct: T2 fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update
fields.Explanation:
At REPEATABLE READ Postgres will not let a transaction update a row changed after its snapshot started. T2 waits for T1, then aborts, and the app must retry.

Silent overwrite is the lost update this level prevents in Postgres (MySQL REPEATABLE READ does allow it with plain reads). Waiting and reapplying is READ COMMITTED. One row and one lock order is not a deadlock.
fields.Hint: The snapshot is older than the row.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: You move a booking flow to Postgres SERIALIZABLE. What must the application add?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, SERIALIZABLE never aborts transactions
Retry the whole transaction when it fails with SQLSTATE 40001
Retry only the statement that failed
A higher lock_timeout
fields.Correct: Retry the whole transaction when it fails with SQLSTATE 40001
fields.Explanation:
SSI aborts transactions that could produce a non-serializable result. The work must be replayed from BEGIN, since the reads it was based on are stale.

Aborts are how SERIALIZABLE works. Retrying one statement keeps the stale reads. Serialization failures are not lock timeouts.
fields.Hint: Expect aborts.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)

fields.Question: Reads go to async replicas. A user saves a new display name, the page reloads, and they see the old name. What is the standard fix?
fields.Choices:
Read that user's own data from the primary for a short window after they write
Put a cache in front of the replicas
Add more replicas
Lower the cache TTL
fields.Correct: Read that user's own data from the primary for a short window after they write
fields.Explanation:
The replica has not applied the write yet. Routing the writer's reads to the primary for a while (or until the replica passes the write's log position) gives read-your-writes without moving all reads.

A cache can also hold the old value and is another lag source. More replicas spread load but each still lags. A TTL does nothing for replication lag.
fields.Hint: Who just wrote?
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
StackScholar: Database replication and sharding interview questions (https://stackscholar.com/system-design-interview/questions/database-replication-and-sharding)

fields.Question: Postgres primary with one asynchronous standby. The primary's disk dies and you promote the standby. What can be lost?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, commits are durable
Only transactions that were still open
All data since the last base backup
Transactions committed on the primary that had not yet reached the standby
fields.Correct: Transactions committed on the primary that had not yet reached the standby
fields.Explanation:
With async replication the primary acknowledges commit before the standby has the WAL. Anything in that gap is gone after promotion.

Durable on the primary's disk does not help when that disk is lost. Open transactions are lost in any setup, the surprise is committed ones. The standby has applied WAL continuously, not only up to the base backup.
fields.Hint: Commit was acknowledged before shipping.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Postgres with synchronous_standby_names set to a single standby and synchronous_commit = on. That standby goes down. What happens to writes on the primary?
fields.Choices:
The primary switches to async automatically
Writes continue and the standby catches up later
Commits wait and hang until a synchronous standby is back or the setting changes
The primary shuts down to protect data
fields.Correct: Commits wait and hang until a synchronous standby is back or the setting changes
fields.Explanation:
Each commit waits for the sync standby's confirmation, so with no standby commits block. That is why setups list two or more candidates or use quorum.

Postgres does not fall back to async on its own. Continuing without confirmation would break the guarantee. The primary keeps running, its commits just wait.
fields.Hint: Synchronous means waiting for an ack.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Synchronous Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html#SYNCHRONOUS-REPLICATION)

fields.Question: A user refreshes and sees a new comment, refreshes again and it is gone, then it reappears. Reads go to random replicas. Which fix targets this specific anomaly?
fields.Choices:
Send all writes through a queue
Pin each user's reads to the same replica
Use synchronous replication for every replica
Shard the comments table
fields.Correct: Pin each user's reads to the same replica
fields.Explanation:
Different replicas lag by different amounts, so random routing can step back in time. Sticking a session to one replica gives monotonic reads.

Queuing writes does not change which replica you read. Synchronous replication slows every commit and, in Postgres, only makes the write visible on the standby with remote_apply. Sharding does not touch read routing.
fields.Hint: Time should not go backwards for one user.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A Postgres primary is at 95% CPU from INSERT and UPDATE traffic, reads are light. Will adding read replicas help?
fields.Choices:
No, every replica still replays all writes and the primary does all of them
Yes, replicas share the write load
Yes, if you use synchronous replication
Yes, if you put the replicas behind a load balancer
fields.Correct: No, every replica still replays all writes and the primary does all of them
fields.Explanation:
Replicas scale reads. Every write still runs on the one primary. For write load you reduce writes, batch them, scale up, or partition and shard.

Single-leader replicas cannot accept writes. Synchronous replication adds latency to writes. A load balancer cannot send writes to a read-only node.
fields.Hint: Who accepts writes?
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)
StackScholar: Database replication and sharding interview questions (https://stackscholar.com/system-design-interview/questions/database-replication-and-sharding)

fields.Question: Chat app: the main query is load the latest 50 messages of a conversation. Messages are sharded by hash(message_id) and that query fans out to every shard. Which shard key fixes it?
fields.Choices:
message_id with a bigger shard count
created_at
sender_id
conversation_id
fields.Correct: conversation_id
fields.Explanation:
Sharding by the key the hot query filters on puts a conversation on one shard, so the read hits one node.

More shards of message_id makes the fan-out wider. created_at puts all new messages on the newest shard. sender_id still spreads one conversation across every participant's shard.
fields.Hint: Shard by what the hot query filters on.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Followers are sharded by hash(user_id). A celebrity with 80M followers makes one shard hot. What helps?
fields.Choices:
Add more shards with the same hash(user_id) key
Switch to range sharding by user_id
Split the hot key across several sub-keys (user_id plus a suffix) and cache its reads
Raise the replication factor of every shard
fields.Correct: Split the hot key across several sub-keys (user_id plus a suffix) and cache its reads
fields.Explanation:
One key always hashes to one shard, however many shards you have. Salting the hot key spreads its writes, and reads gather the sub-keys or come from cache.

Adding shards moves other keys, not the one hot key. Range sharding still keeps a single user_id on one shard. More replicas can help reads but not writes to one key.
fields.Hint: One key maps to one shard.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-sharding.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: An events store is range-sharded by created_at. What problem shows up under steady ingest?
fields.Choices:
Reads for recent events fan out to every shard
All new writes land on the shard holding the newest range
Range queries by time become impossible
Shards get rebalanced on every insert
fields.Correct: All new writes land on the shard holding the newest range
fields.Explanation:
Monotonic keys make the newest range a single write hotspot. Prefix with a well-spread key (for example source_id) and keep time as the second part.

Recent events are on one shard, the opposite of fan-out. Time ranges are exactly what range sharding is good at. Splits happen as ranges grow, not per insert.
fields.Hint: Where does now live?
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Designing partition keys to distribute your workload (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-uniform-load.html)

fields.Question: Keys are placed with hash(key) mod N. You go from 4 shards to 5. Roughly what fraction of keys must move?
fields.Choices:
About 80%
About 20%
About 25%
None, only new keys go to shard 5
fields.Correct: About 80%
fields.Explanation:
A key stays only if hash mod 4 equals hash mod 5, which is true for 4 of every 20 residues, so about 80% move. Consistent hashing moves about 1/5 instead.

About 20% is the consistent hashing figure. 25% confuses it with the old shard count. With mod N the placement of existing keys changes as soon as N changes.
fields.Hint: Compare h mod 4 with h mod 5.
fields.Source:
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees, Karger et al., 1997 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: A single Postgres primary: 300 GB, 3,000 queries per second, 35% CPU, p99 creeping up from a few slow queries. The team proposes sharding. What is the best next step?
fields.Choices:
Shard now by user_id, before the data gets larger
Move to a NoSQL database
Shard by table, one database per table
Fix the slow queries and indexes, and add read replicas or a bigger box before sharding
fields.Correct: Fix the slow queries and indexes, and add read replicas or a bigger box before sharding
fields.Explanation:
This load fits a single node well. Sharding adds cross-shard queries, transactions and rebalancing for no gain here, while the actual problem is a few slow queries.

Sharding early pays the complexity cost years ahead. Changing database type does not fix bad queries. Splitting by table breaks joins and does not address the slow queries.
fields.Hint: Is the box actually full?
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)

fields.Question: Users are sharded by user_id. How do you move money between two users on different shards?
fields.Answer:
Avoid 2PC across shards if you can: it blocks while the coordinator is down and holds locks across the network. Use a saga: debit the sender with an idempotent ledger entry and an outbox event, then credit the receiver idempotently using the transfer id, with a compensating credit if the second step fails permanently.

Keep a transfer row with its state so retries and reconciliation can find stuck transfers. If such transfers are frequent, reconsider the shard key so related accounts live together.
fields.Hint: Saga with idempotent steps, not distributed locks.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
Pattern: Transactional outbox, Chris Richardson, microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)

fields.Question: DynamoDB. Access pattern: get a customer's orders, newest first, paged. Which key design fits?
fields.Choices:
Partition key order_id and a Scan with a filter on customer_id
Partition key order_date, sort key customer_id
Partition key customer_id, sort key order_date#order_id
Partition key customer_id with no sort key
fields.Correct: Partition key customer_id, sort key order_date#order_id
fields.Explanation:
A Query on the customer's partition returns its items in sort key order, and ScanIndexForward = false gives newest first with paging.

A Scan reads the whole table. order_date as partition key spreads one customer over many dates and makes today hot. Without a sort key each customer can have only one item.
fields.Hint: Partition by who, sort by when.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/best-practices.html)
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)

fields.Question: A DynamoDB Query on a partition reads 1 MB of items and a FilterExpression keeps 5 of them. What do you pay for?
fields.Choices:
Only the 5 items returned
The full 1 MB read, because filters apply after items are read
Nothing extra, filters use an index
Half, filtered items are discounted
fields.Correct: The full 1 MB read, because filters apply after items are read
fields.Explanation:
Read capacity is charged for items read before filtering. If you filter often on an attribute, make it part of a key or a GSI.

Paying only for returned items is the common assumption and it is wrong. FilterExpression does not use an index. There is no discount for filtered items.
fields.Hint: Filtering happens after the read.
fields.Source: Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/best-practices.html)

fields.Question: A payments ledger needs multi-row atomic transfers, strong constraints, and finance's ad hoc reporting queries. Scale is 500 writes per second. Which store fits?
fields.Choices:
A relational database such as PostgreSQL
A wide-column store such as Cassandra
A document store, one document per account
A key-value cache such as Redis as the primary store
fields.Correct: A relational database such as PostgreSQL
fields.Explanation:
Transactions across rows, constraints and ad hoc SQL are what relational databases do, and 500 writes per second is light load.

Cassandra is tuned for huge write volume on known queries, with weak multi-row transactions and no ad hoc joins. One document per account makes transfers cross-document. Redis as the primary ledger has weaker durability and no reporting.
fields.Hint: Read the requirements, not the hype.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A feed is read 100 times per write, so you copy author_name into every post row to skip a join. What cost do you accept?
fields.Choices:
Reads become slower
You can no longer index posts
Writes of new posts need a distributed transaction
A name change must update every post, and copies can be stale in the meantime
fields.Correct: A name change must update every post, and copies can be stale in the meantime
fields.Explanation:
Denormalising trades write work and consistency for cheaper reads. Renames fan out to many rows, usually async, so some posts show the old name for a while.

Reads get faster, that is the point. Indexes still work. A new post copies the name at insert in a single write.
fields.Hint: Copies have to be kept in sync.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
Hello Interview: Core Concepts for System Design (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/core-concepts)

fields.Question: Model a chat app in DynamoDB that must list a user's conversations by latest activity and page the messages in a conversation.
fields.Answer:
Messages: partition key conversation_id, sort key a time-ordered message id, then Query newest first with a limit. Inbox: an item per user and conversation with partition key user_id and sort key last_activity#conversation_id, updated on each message (fan out per participant). Start from access patterns, not entities.

Big group chats make the inbox fan-out expensive, so cap it or read group activity lazily. A very hot conversation may need write sharding.
fields.Hint: List access patterns first, then choose keys.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/best-practices.html)
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Designing partition keys to distribute your workload (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-uniform-load.html)

fields.Question: A storage engine calls write() on its log and gets success. Which failure can still lose that record?
fields.Choices:
A crash of the process itself
Nothing, write() means it is on disk
Power loss before fsync, since the data may only be in the OS page cache
Only a disk failure
fields.Correct: Power loss before fsync, since the data may only be in the OS page cache
fields.Explanation:
write() copies data into the kernel's page cache. The kernel still holds it if the process dies, but power loss or a kernel crash before fsync drops it.

A process crash does not erase the page cache. write() returning is not durability. Disk failure is a separate risk, the trap here is the cache.
fields.Hint: Where does write() put the bytes?
fields.Source:
Linux man page: fsync(2) (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)
PracHub: Design a crash resilient LRU cache (https://prachub.com/interview-questions/design-a-crash-resilient-lru-cache)

fields.Question: Postgres acknowledges a COMMIT, then the machine loses power before the changed data pages reach disk. Why is the change not lost?
fields.Choices:
Data pages are written synchronously on every commit
The WAL record was flushed to disk before COMMIT returned, and recovery replays it
The standby always has a copy
The OS flushes the page cache on power loss
fields.Correct: The WAL record was flushed to disk before COMMIT returned, and recovery replays it
fields.Explanation:
With synchronous_commit on, Postgres flushes WAL up to the commit record before acknowledging. Data pages are written later by checkpoints, and crash recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint.

Writing data pages on every commit is what WAL avoids. A standby is optional and may be async. A power loss cannot flush RAM.
fields.Hint: Log first, pages later.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html)

fields.Question: You set synchronous_commit = off on a Postgres server to speed up writes. What is the risk?
fields.Choices:
The last fraction of a second of acknowledged commits can be lost on a crash, but the database stays consistent
The database can be corrupted after a crash
Replicas stop receiving changes
Nothing, it only affects replication
fields.Correct: The last fraction of a second of acknowledged commits can be lost on a crash, but the database stays consistent
fields.Explanation:
COMMIT returns before the WAL flush, so a crash loses up to about three times wal_writer_delay of recent commits. Unlike fsync = off, it cannot corrupt data.

Corruption is the fsync = off risk. Replication still runs. The setting governs local WAL flush too, not only standbys.
fields.Hint: Compare it with fsync = off.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Write Ahead Log settings (synchronous_commit, fsync) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html)

fields.Question: A new report query takes 30 seconds. Each app instance has a 20 connection pool. Soon every API endpoint times out, even ones that do not touch the report. What stops the cascade first?
fields.Choices:
Raise each pool from 20 to 500 connections
Add read replicas for all endpoints
Restart the app servers on a schedule
A statement_timeout plus fixing or isolating the slow query
fields.Correct: A statement_timeout plus fixing or isolating the slow query
fields.Explanation:
Slow queries hold pooled connections, so other requests wait on the pool and time out. Capping statement time frees connections, and the report gets fixed or moved to its own pool or a replica.

Bigger pools let more slow queries pile onto the database and slow everything. Replicas do not stop a slow query hogging a pool. Restarts only reset the problem.
fields.Hint: Who is holding the connections?
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Client Connection Defaults (statement and lock timeouts) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html)
HikariCP: About Pool Sizing (https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing)

fields.Question: 50 app instances each want a 100 connection pool, so the team plans max_connections = 5000 on one Postgres server. What is the better approach?
fields.Choices:
Set max_connections = 5000, Postgres scales linearly with connections
Open a new connection per request instead of pooling
Keep pools small and put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres
Give each instance one connection
fields.Correct: Keep pools small and put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres
fields.Explanation:
Each Postgres connection is a process with memory overhead, and throughput peaks at a modest number of active connections. A pooler multiplexes many clients over few server connections.

Thousands of active backends cause context switching and lock contention. Connecting per request adds setup latency and still spikes connections. One connection per instance serialises all requests.
fields.Hint: More connections is not more throughput.
fields.Source:
HikariCP: About Pool Sizing (https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing)
PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)

fields.Question: Items are written to Postgres and copied to Elasticsearch through CDC. A user creates an item and it is missing from search for a few seconds. What is the right response?
fields.Choices:
Write to Postgres and Elasticsearch in one transaction
Accept it as expected lag, and show the user's new item from the database or the write response
Make the CDC pipeline synchronous with the request
Poll Elasticsearch until the item appears before returning
fields.Correct: Accept it as expected lag, and show the user's new item from the database or the write response
fields.Explanation:
CDC is asynchronous by design. Product-wise, the creator sees their item from the source of truth while search catches up.

There is no shared transaction across Postgres and Elasticsearch. A synchronous pipeline couples request latency to the search cluster. Polling adds latency and still fails when the pipeline is behind.
fields.Hint: Search is a derived copy.
fields.Source:
Debezium Documentation: PostgreSQL connector (https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/connectors/postgresql.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: An endpoint's p99 went from 80 ms to 2 s after a deploy. How do you find the database cause?
fields.Answer:
Check pg_stat_statements for queries whose total or mean time jumped, and pg_stat_activity for waiting sessions and lock waits. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the suspect query and compare estimated with actual rows and look for seq scans or sorts.

Common causes: a new query pattern without an index, an N+1 loop, stale statistics after a bulk load, lock contention from a migration, pool exhaustion. Fix, then confirm with the same metrics.
fields.Hint: Measure, then EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
